Having a key individual champion for the adoption of adaptive lighting is crucial. The main resistance to adoption came from law enforcement and individuals who believed that brighter 78 lights equated to better safety. Engagement with electric utilities can vary, but their support and partnership are necessary, especially if they own the streetlights. While there is no “How to Why to” guide for adopting adaptive lighting technology, the best practice would involve a customized checklist or questionnaire to determine the unique aspects of each city, including their lighting needs, fiber connectivity, and wireless signal strength. The respondents suggested the importance of gathering more information and pursuing more options in the marketplace to ensure the success of the implementation process. Overall, the difficulties in trust experienced in adopting adaptive lighting technology would also apply to other smart city technologies. Having more standards and guidelines from organizations like IES, AASHTO, and FHWA would be helpful. The respondents suggested considering different communication protocols and vetting the network control system specification. Finally, they highlighted the importance of showing the benefits in terms of savings and energy to ensure continued support from stakeholders. 4.2.4 Surveys of Residents 4.2.4.1 Results Overall, more than half (57%) of the respondents indicated that they had not been contacted by the city prior to implementing adaptive lighting policy in their city or town. Approximately 35% of respondents did know whether they had been contacted or not.
